settings.title: A Nerve You've Never Heard Of
settings.text: The posterior tibial nerve runs from the inner ankle to the sacral nerve center (S2-S4) in your lower spine. This nerve center controls your bladder: when to squeeze, when to relax. Every trip to the bathroom, every hold, every release is governed by signals traveling this pathway.

settings.title: When the Signal Misfires
settings.text:
During menopause, hormonal changes cause this nerve signal to misfire. Your bladder receives false "squeeze" signals, making it think it's full when it's not. Every urgent trip, every nighttime wake-up: it's the signal, not the bladder.

Think of it like a fire alarm going off when there's no fire. Your bladder isn't weak or damaged. It's responding to a faulty signal telling it to squeeze when it shouldn't.

settings.title: Clinics Have Been Treating This for 20+ Years
settings.text:
Urologists use a procedure called PTNS: a thin needle at the inner ankle sends gentle electrical pulses up this nerve to calm the overactive signal. It's backed by randomized controlled trials with thousands of participants.

The catch: 12 weekly clinic visits. $3,000 to $5,000 out of pocket. Most insurance doesn't cover it. And most women never hear about it in the first place.
Based on the same science used in urology clinics worldwide. No needle. No office visits. Same nerve. Same principle.

settings.heading: How long before I see results?
settings.row_content: Studies show improvement beginning around 4-6 weeks with consistent use (3-4 sessions per week, 30 minutes each). Some women notice changes sooner. For best results, use consistently for at least 60 days.

settings.heading: How is this different from a regular TENS unit?
settings.row_content: Tibella uses a specific frequency (20 Hz), pulse width (200 microseconds), and placement protocol designed for the posterior tibial nerve. A regular back pain TENS unit doesn't target this nerve pathway. This isn't general pain relief. It targets a specific nerve for a specific purpose.

settings.heading: Will it work if medications didn't?
settings.row_content: Tibella works through a completely different mechanism. Medications suppress the bladder signal with chemicals, which is why they come with side effects. Tibella targets the nerve pathway directly. Studies have shown improvement even in women who didn't respond to medication.

settings.heading: Is it uncomfortable?
settings.row_content: Most users describe a gentle tingling sensation. You control the intensity across 19 levels, so you can always find a comfortable setting. Zero side effects were reported in clinical trials of surface-electrode tibial nerve stimulation.

settings.heading: Can I use it with my current medications or HRT?
settings.row_content: Yes. Tibella is non-invasive and non-pharmacological. It works alongside any existing treatment, including hormone replacement therapy and OAB medications. Always consult with your healthcare provider if you have questions about your specific situation.
